content.tldr: The meeting focused on GitLab's scaling strategy, comparing functional decomposition (2x scaling) with a podding approach (potential 10x-33x scaling). Preliminary data showing 97% of users interact with only one top-level namespace strongly supports pursuing the podding strategy for significant scaling benefits.

bullets.text: Josh is documenting high-level strategy, iteration strategies, and non-detest options, and gathering data on cross-namespace workflows.
Principles for the scaling work, including minimizing self-managed impact, have been documented.
Functional decomposition of CI data is estimated to provide a 2x scaling benefit.
Preliminary data indicates 97% of users interact with only one top-level namespace, suggesting potential for 33x scaling with pods.
Podding offers a significant benefit by allowing GitLab to be its own biggest customer, identifying issues before they impact other pods.
Josh is documenting high-level strategy, iteration strategies, and non-detest options.
Data is being gathered on cross-namespace workflows.
Principles for the work, including minimizing self-managed impact, have been documented on slide three.
Josh reflowed initial slides for clearer narrative and added a slide on why sharding within a pod is not needed.
Eric believes functional decomposition is relevant for large self-managed customers and should be a "forever decision."
Sid stated functional decomposition of CI data provides a 2x scaling benefit, while the overall problem is 10x.
Jarir clarified functional decomposition was always intended as a bridge to sharding, not a long-term strategy for everything.
Sid expressed concern that decomposition discussions are leading towards microservices complexity and two-phase commits.
Fabienne confirmed current decomposition work is solely focused on CI tables, with no decisions made for other parts.
Sid emphasized the goal is 10x scaling for 10 million users, which decomposition alone cannot achieve.
The core question is whether to shard via pods or table shards, as decomposition might complicate a pod strategy.
Fabienne presented preliminary data showing 97% of all users interact with only one top-level namespace.
For users with paid namespaces, 97% interact with two or fewer top-level namespaces.
Sid interpreted this as potential for 33x scaling if 3% of users need to be in the same pod.
Fabienne noted limitations: data is across all users (not active), personal namespaces are not separated, and reasons for low cross-namespace usage are unclear.
Sid suggested even if 10% of users need to be on the same pods, it still offers 10x headroom.
Josh added that the value of cross-namespace workflows might be low, so disrupting them might not significantly alter user experience.
Steve highlighted that dedicating a pod for GitLab's own use helped find many problems before they reached other customer pods.
Sid agreed this is a great point and should be added to the slide deck.
Fabienne will get an estimate from the CI decomposition team on expected headroom.
Fabienne will run a report on what percentage of all namespaces the 3% of users (who use more than one namespace) are spread across.
Sid asked to add the benefit of using a dedicated pod for GitLab's own use to the slide deck.

content.tldr: The meeting compared functional decomposition against a podding strategy for scaling GitLab to 10 million users. Preliminary data showing 97% of users stay within one namespace suggests podding offers significantly higher scaling potential than decomposition.

bullets.text: Josh is documenting high-level strategy, iteration plans, and principles for the podding project.
Fabienne and the database group found that 97% of all users interact with only one top-level namespace.
The CI decomposition team is currently focused solely on CI tables to address immediate scaling constraints.
The team will maintain the single data store strategy for acquisitions rather than integrating separate decomposed databases.
A dedicated internal pod will be added to the production deployment chain to identify issues before they reach customers.
Sid expressed concern that functional decomposition adds excessive application complexity and baggage to the codebase.
Steve warned that podding alone may eventually be insufficient for the largest accounts, requiring further data decomposition.
Current database proposals, such as normalizing certain tables, may make future podding or splitting more difficult.

How would disrupting cross-namespace workflows, like forking open-source projects, impact the overall user experience?
Fabienne will analyze the distribution of the 3% of cross-namespace users across the total project landscape.
Fabienne will obtain a formal estimate from the decomposition team regarding expected database headroom gains.
Josh will update the slide deck to include the benefits of using internal pods for early bug detection.

chapters.title: Meeting Start & Updates
chapters.gist: Josh provided updates on investigation streams, documentation for high-level strategy, and refinements to the presentation slides.

chapters.title: Decomposition vs. Podding Strategy
chapters.gist: Eric and Sid debated the benefits of functional decomposition for self-managed customers and CI data, questioning its scaling impact compared to podding.

chapters.title: Clarifying Decomposition's Role
chapters.gist: Jarir clarified that functional decomposition was intended as a bridge to sharding, not a long-term strategy, to reduce sharding complexity and create boundaries.

chapters.title: Cross-Namespace Workflow Data
chapters.gist: Fabienne presented preliminary data indicating that 97% of users interact with only one top-level namespace, suggesting significant scaling potential for podding.

chapters.title: Podding Benefits & Conclusion
chapters.gist: Steve highlighted the operational benefits of using a dedicated pod for internal use, and the meeting concluded with appreciation for the discussion.
